# Hardware Debug

## Concepts

Debug improves observability and control but also creates access to architectural state. Define who may halt a processor, inspect memory, alter registers, or access protected peripherals, and in which lifecycle states those actions are permitted.

Functional verification, manufacturing test, and runtime debug serve different purposes. Scan chains and BIST help identify fabricated defects; debug helps investigate executing systems. Their access paths can nevertheless overlap with security-sensitive state.

## Implementation

Create a threat model listing assets, entry points, allowed users, and required isolation. Include debug ports, buses, reset controls, and test modes. Identify whether these paths can bypass normal privilege checks.

For a RISC-V SoC, trace debug access through the processor and interconnect using the actual implementation. Check the selected CORE-V Wally configuration before assigning a security policy to the debug interface. Specify reset and lock behavior, including whether a locked setting can be reopened.

## Hands-on Experiments

Add tests for allowed and rejected debug transactions in each modeled state. Attempt a protected register access through both the normal bus and the debug path. Check behavior during reset and when configuration locks are set.

Inject a selected control-state fault in simulation and classify the result: detected, contained, silently corrupted, or an access-control violation. Record what the experiment models and what it cannot establish about physical attacks.
